title: The PROPEL Folio: Grade the Judgment, Not the Essay
author: Terry U.
summary: Writing under the byline "terryu," this essay revisits a 1989 teacher-research finding by Jim Hahn about the classroom "handback" moment, when students receive graded essays back and often ignore or misunderstand the teacher's comments once a grade is visible. The author traces later attempts to fix this problem by delaying the grade (Kristy Louden, Marcus Luther) and contrasts them with a more radical approach: Roberta Camp's Arts PROPEL portfolio project, which asked students to develop their own evaluative judgment rather than simply wait for a teacher's verdict. Building on Arts PROPEL's model of collection, selection, and reflection, the author proposes a five-month, PROPEL-inspired portfolio design in which individual pieces of writing are not graded; instead, the final grade attaches to students' demonstrated ability to select evidence and argue for their own development as writers across the term. The piece situates this proposal within the decades-old teacher-research tradition and closes with Kathryn Howard's practice of sending student portfolios home so parents learn to read for growth and pattern rather than a single grade.
points: Jim Hahn's 1989 teacher-research study on the 'handback' moment found many students ignored or couldn't explain teacher comments once a grade was visible, revealing a mismatch between teachers' assumptions and student behavior.
Kristy Louden and Marcus Luther's classroom experiments show that simply delaying the grade increases attention to feedback but does not change who holds evaluative authority.
Roberta Camp's Arts PROPEL portfolio project reframes assessment as 'an episode of learning' by having students collect, select, and reflect on their own writing before receiving a verdict.

The author proposes a five-month classroom experiment built on monthly selections (Problem Piece, Surprise Piece, Unsatisfying Piece, Satisfying Piece) culminating in a portfolio argument, with the final grade measuring the quality of the student's self-assessment rather than any single essay.
Kathryn Howard's practice of sending portfolios home taught parents to ask 'How is the writing going?' instead of 'What grade did you get?', extending the reflective practice into the family.
quotes: When a student receives a judgment, the student does not make a judgment.

we were not terribly surprised that they came into the school year expecting that the teacher would tell them what was good or not so good in their work, and that their job would be to understand and accept the teacher’s judgment.
The student still waits for the verdict. The teacher still decides what is good or not so good.
Note well: This system cannot be easily gamed by AI. How would AI know what satisfied a writer?
A student who selects a technically weak piece and gives a careful, self-aware account of why it matters may outscore a student who selects polished work and can say only, “I like it.
The handback loop begins to close when the person waiting at home stops asking, “What grade did you get?” and starts asking, “How is the writing going?
This does more than delay a grade until comments have been read. It restructures what the grade measures.
